x.name: Ryo Lu
x.bio: Designed @Cursor_ai, @NotionHQ, @Stripe, built startups. I make a world where anyone can make software. Aspiring k-pop idol.

tweets.text: https://t.co/9JFKOz3lEv

augmenting human intellect

when i started making software, i wasn’t dreaming of a factory.

i loved that something on a screen could become an extension of my mind. a place to put a thought before i understood it. to move things around until new connections appeared. to make little systems that worked the way i worked, even if it made no sense to anyone else.

the computer wasn’t interesting because it could do work without me. it was interesting because of what i could do with it.

the early lineage of computing was built around this possibility. in 1962, Engelbart described augmenting human intellect as helping a person understand complex situations and find solutions that were previously out of reach. his starting point was the human being, not the autonomous machine.

he wasn’t describing a faster black box. he was looking at the whole relationship between a person, their tools, their language, their methods, and what they could learn to do with them. the capability belonged to that whole system.

somewhere along the way, we started telling a much smaller story about a much more powerful technology.

more automation. more agents. more software producing more software. more output from fewer people. more growth. more numbers to prove that something is happening.

and less attention to the person any of this is supposed to be for.

i don’t want to pretend computing had a pure innocent beginning. replacing human labor was one of its ambitions. even in 1960, Licklider distinguished human-computer symbiosis from systems where the remaining people mainly served the machine. he wanted computers to participate in the formation of ideas, not only execute problems already defined.

that distinction feels important – does the system help you discover what you mean? or does it only want you to submit a request, and wait outside while it works?

sometimes waiting is exactly what i want. please do the search. move the files. take away the repetitive work.

but not everything difficult is overhead.

sometimes moving the pieces around is how you understand them. sometimes making the thing changes what you wanted to make. sometimes you need to see the wrong version, touch it, take it apart, and discover a better question.

i want tools that leave room for that relationship.

in his 1981 paper on Smalltalk, Ingalls described a system meant to support everyone’s creative spirit. personal mastery mattered: an individual should be able to comprehend the system, rather than remain dependent on something permanently beyond their reach.

he also argued that computer models should fit the human mind, rather than demand the reverse.

not one perfect workflow for everyone. systems that different people can inhabit differently. someone who thinks through pictures. someone who needs to write. someone who understands a problem by building a simulation. someone whose way of organizing their life doesn’t resemble a SaaS dashboard.

a system you can reshape as your understanding changes.

this is what i want AI to make possible. not just pumping out software, but having a living relationship with it. being able to ask why something works this way. change one part without surrendering the rest. see what happened. undo it. learn enough to make the next change yourself.

the machine can become more capable without making the person smaller.

but that won’t happen just because we make the models better. we have to care about it. design for it. notice when we are making someone more dependent while calling it empowerment.

i don’t want to measure the future only by how much work happens without us.

i want to know what becomes possible for the person who couldn’t participate before.

what can they understand now? what can they express? what can they change without asking permission?

when i say augmenting human intellect, that is what i mean.

not a world that no longer needs us.
a world we have more ability to shape.

x.bio: AI for the world’s most complex legal work.

tweets.text:
When a judge raised a pivotal question during a major tax dispute, a @ClaytonUtz lawyer found the answer in Harvey in just 40 seconds.

See how the firm uses Harvey to make critical information accessible when it matters most: https://t.co/Oa2baeYWFm https://t.co/DOR6lcsJY2

Harvey now enforces ethical walls using client matters and policies synced from @imanageinc Security Policy Manager (“SPM”).

Harvey respects the information barriers a firm already has, so lawyers can collaborate without a second set of rules to manage.

Read more: https://t.co/OzabZhOqar

Next, we plan to open-source our environment-building pipeline and basic pairwise grader, enabling researchers to construct their own case law environments and study these capabilities.

Full findings and methodology: https://t.co/EvCefSuqkF

What we found:

A small group of frontier models can now research and write complete, first-draft briefs in a single shot, moving substantially closer to the high bar for filing with a court. But even the strongest still fall short of that bar, with issues like hallucinations and reliance on decisions that have been set aside.

How LAB: USCL works:

We built 100 environments from public federal dockets collected by @freelawproject, spanning trial and appellate courts, every stage of motion briefing, and more than ten areas of law. Model-written briefs face off head-to-head, and wins and losses roll up into Elo ratings.

During our leadership offsite, a customer described feeling like models were hitting legal AGI.

Our new research in LAB: US Case Law is focused on confirming that claim for one of the longest-horizon litigation tasks: researching and writing briefs.

We find that the recent frontier models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra show emerging capabilities to complete this task in ways comparable to experts and in conditions where previous models would clearly fail.

They still need supervision and review to be ready to file, but it feels like we’ve hit the inflection point that coding hit a year ago when engineers went from writing model-assisted code to supervising agent outputs at scale.

Excited to welcome @piyprah @atishdassarma and the rest of the @get_aida team to Harvey.

Piyush co-founded Glean and we met a couple years ago when he was starting Aida.

At Aida, they were building Harvey for sales and a lot of the product and infrastructure they were building was things we had been planning.

He became someone I regularly turned to for advice when I was thinking through enterprise search and related technical strategies.

A couple months ago when we decided to focus more on these efforts they were the first team we turned to to help lead these.

Together we're going to build each firm its own ontology: a private context layer that connects all of its data and turns it into IP the firm owns.

That context makes every agent and model and product the firm uses better and stays private and portable through our APIs and will be able to run on-prem for firms that want full control.

A firm's context is its edge and the firms that own theirs will be the ones that stand apart.

LAB: US Case Law

We’re extending Harvey’s Legal Agent Bench to US case law, with 100 environments built from real federal dockets spanning 10+ areas of law.

Long-form writing matters for long-horizon agent research, especially in verticals with a significant degree of domain expertise like law.

Brief writing combines research, analysis, and drafting across hundreds of pages of source material. An agent has to preserve the evidence behind each claim through context compaction and use it correctly as it develops an argument. Errors during research or pre-writing phases compound and can carry over into the final draft.

Models are getting much better at producing complete first drafts, as evidenced in the video attached video, but there's still a lot of headroom to go!
https://t.co/fEzypW71HO
